name: Goodbye Souvenir
description: I won't feel lonely, nor will I be sorrowful... not before everything is buried. A string of n beads is left as the message of leaving. The beads are numbered from 1 to n from left to right, each having a shape numbered by integers between 1 and n inclusive. Some beads may have the same shapes. The memory of a shape x in a certain subsegment of beads, is defined to be the difference between the last position and the first position that shape x appears in the segment. The memory of a subsegment is the sum of memories over all shapes that occur in it. From time to time, shapes of beads change as well as the memories . Sometimes, the past secreted in subsegments are being recalled, and you are to find the memory for each of them.
input_specification: The first line of input contains two space-separated integers n and m ( 1 ≤ n , m ≤ 100 000 ) — the number of beads in the string, and the total number of changes and queries, respectively. The second line contains n integers a 1 , a 2 , ..., a n ( 1 ≤ a i ≤ n ) — the initial shapes of beads 1, 2, ..., n , respectively. The following m lines each describes either a change in the beads or a query of subsegment. A line has one of the following formats: 1 p x ( 1 ≤ p ≤ n , 1 ≤ x ≤ n ), meaning that the shape of the p -th bead is changed into x ; 2 l r ( 1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n ), denoting a query of memory of the subsegment from l to r , inclusive.
output_specification: For each query, print one line with an integer — the memory of the recalled subsegment.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 848C — Goodbye Souvenir [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
